newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Main trade powers look for telecom deal by weekend.
newsitem.headline: Main trade powers look for telecom deal by weekend.

text.p: Senior officials from the world's four main trading powers on Tuesday discussed clinching a global pact to liberalise the $600 billion telecommunications market by its Saturday deadline, officials said.

U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang and Robert Verrue, director-general of telecommunications for the European Union (EU), were joined by Canada's Assistant Minister of Industry Michael Binder and Akemi Yamaguchi, Japan's deputy minister of telecommunications.
The so-called "Quad" talks were held for several hours behind closed doors at the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which is sponsoring the negotiations. Bilateral meetings followed.
Some 59 governments representing more than 90 per cent of the global market have submitted offers to open their domestic telecom markets to foreign operators.
Sri Lanka and Tanzania were expected to present offers by the end of the week, according to WTO sources.

"The U.S. is not looking to write down or change its offer. We are focusing our attention on improving other offers to the point that the talks are an overall success," an American official in Geneva told Reuters.
"We are waiting to see what responses will be," he added. "Things are close but it is not a done deal."
U.S. negotiators were believed to be concentrating on wresting improvements from South Korea, Canada and Mexico, according to trade sources.
To a lesser extent, Brazil and India were also being pressured to make further concessions.
Chances of clinching a deal are seen to depend on Washington's assessment of whether a "critical mass" of offers have been presented, according to trade sources.
The United States -- the world's largest market -- derailed an effort last April to reach a global pact when it backed away saying offers from emerging economies were insufficient.
Lang told reporters on Monday he saw progress towards agreement, but important issues remained to be solved.

He said that Washington was not satisfied with the extent to which Canada had offered to open its telecom companies to foreign ownership. Ottawa's offer allows a maximum of 47.8 per cent of equity capital to be held by non-Canadians.
